div.p: To unravel how within-person psychological processes fluctuate in daily life, and how these processes differ between persons, intensive longitudinal (IL) designs in which participants are repeatedly measured, have become popular. Commonly used statistical models for those designs are multilevel models with autocorrelated errors. Substantive hypotheses of interest are then typically investigated via statistical hypotheses tests for model parameters of interest. An important question in the design of such IL studies concerns the determination of the number of participants and the number of measurements per person needed to achieve sufficient statistical power for those statistical tests. Recent advances in computational methods and software enabled the computation of statistical power using Monte Carlo simulations. However, this approach is computationally intensive and, therefore, quite restrictive. To ease power computations, we derive simple-to-use analytical formulas for multilevel models with AR(1) within-person errors. Analytic expressions for a model family are obtained via asymptotic approximations of all sample statistics in the precision matrix of the fixed effects. To validate this analytical approach to power computation, we compare it to the simulation-based approach via a series of Monte Carlo simulations. We find comparable performances making the analytic approach a useful tool for researchers that can drastically save them time and resources.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In recent years, many researchers conducted intensive longitudinal (IL) studies (see e.g., Ariens et al., 2020;Eisele et al., 2022;Mestdagh and Dejonckheere, 2021;Myin-Germeys et al., 2009, 2018). These studies are characterized by repeated measurement occasions nested within individuals. Such datasets are commonly used in investigations of a wide variety of theories and research hypotheses related to how within-person psychological processes fluctuate in daily life, and how these processes differ between persons. In particular, researchers often investigate inter-group or inter-personal differences in the mean level of a time-varying target outcome, within-person effects of time-varying predictors, and interaction effects between time-varying and invariant predictors (see e.g., Heininga et al., 2019;Dejonckheere et al., 2018;Myin-Germeys et al., 2003). Typically, these research questions are investigated by fitting multilevel (or mixed-effects) regression models to the IL data and by conducting statistical hypotheses tests for the model parameters (see Raudenbush and Bryk (2002) for an introduction to multilevel modeling). These models account for the nested structure of the data by allowing some or all regression coefficients (i.e., intercepts and slopes) to vary across persons. Thus, this model estimates fixed effects (i.e., the average intercept or slope across persons) and random effects, which represent how person-specific intercepts or slopes deviate from the corresponding fixed effect.

As previously stated, IL data is characterized by repeated measurements that are closer in time, implying some form of dependence between measurements. Thus, when modeling IL data, neglecting the serial dependence by using traditional regression models may introduce misspecification biases (Ariens et al., 2023). For multilevel models applied to IL data, a common way of handling the serial dependency between the repeated measurements is to assume the within-person errors to be serially correlated through an AR(1) process (Goldstein et al., 1994). Failing to account for the serial dependency by ignoring that within-person errors are serially correlated can lead to overestimation of the variance of the random effects and standard errors of the fixed effects estimates (see e.g., Ferron et al., 2002;Kwok et al., 2007). Therefore, in this paper, we centered our attention on multilevel models with autocorrelated errors.

When designing an IL study it is important to have an idea about statistical power for the to-be-tested statistical hypotheses, to inform sample size decisions (Lakens, 2022). In IL studies, the sample size is determined by both the number of participants and the number of measurements per participant. Statistical power is then defined as the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is true in the population under study (Cohen, 2013). The statistical power to detect a hypothesized effect is determined by the size of the effect in the population, the predetermined type I error rate (i.e., the significance level), and the standard error of the test statistic used. Power is higher if the population effect is larger, the type I error rate is higher, and the standard error of the test statistic is smaller. The standard error is defined as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the test statistic and it is a function of both the true values of the parameters of the model considered and the sample size of the study.

For many non-IL models, a priori (i.e., before collecting the data) power computations can be done by making use of analytical formulas for computing the standard error of the test statistic, which form the backbone of widely used software packages such as G*Power (Faul et al., 2007).

Even though a priori power analysis is the most common approach for deciding on sample size (Lakens, 2022), most of the published empirical studies that use IL designs do not explicitly report having done one. For example, a recent review found that only 2% of the articles published between 2012 and 2018 in the field of daily life research on psychopathology explicitly reported a power analysis (Trull and Ebner-Priemer, 2020). This may be explained by the fact that analytical formulas (see e.g., Hedeker et al. (1999); Moerbeek et al. (2000); Moerbeek et al. (2001); Moerbeek and Maas (2005); Raudenbush (1997); Raudenbush and Liu (2001); Snijders and Bosker (1993); Wang et al. (2015)) for the computation of power are model specific and have not yet been derived for models that explicitly account for the serial dependency that characterizes IL data. These issues are discussed in detail in Arend and Schäfer (2019), Lafit et al. (2021), and Murayama et al. (2022). Furthermore, ignoring the serial dependency in the within-person errors can yield underpowered IL studies due to the overestimation of the standard errors of the fixed effects estimates which lower statistical power (Kwok et al., 2007).

The so-called simulation-based approach provides a workaround. This approach gained popularity because it does not require the derivation of complex formulas for the standard error(s) of the used test statistic(s) (see Arend and Schäfer (2019) for an overview). To compute statistical power for a fixed effect of interest, a researcher can use the simulationbased approach as follows. First, the researcher selects a multilevel model and plausible values of its parameters (see Lafit et al. (2021Lafit et al. ( , 2022)); Lane and Hennes (2018) for a discussion on how to determine plausible values for the parameters of multilevel models for computing statistical power) and the number of participants and measurements per participant. Using these values a large number of data sets are simulated. Each of these data sets is then used to fit the multilevel model and test the hypothesis of interest. Finally, statistical power is estimated as the percentage of generated datasets in which the null hypothesis of interest was rejected at the selected alpha level.

The simulation-based approach has the advantage that it can always be applied no matter how complicated the parametric statistical model of interest is. Researchers can easily implement this approach due to the availability of step-by-step tutorials and open-source applications (Arend and Schäfer (2019); Astivia et al. (2019); Bolger (2011); Browne et al. (2009); Green and MacLeod (2016); Lafit et al. (2021); Lafit et al. (2022)). Although these resources are a crucial addition to the toolkit of IL researchers, they have the downside of being computationally intensive. When the goal is to conduct a power analysis to select the number of persons, for a fixed number of repeated measurement occasions, the computational time can increase considerably since statistical power is computed by conducting Monte Carlo simulations varying the number of persons. This issue is exacerbated when varying both the number of persons and the number of repeated measurements per person. For example, in the illustrations included in Lafit et al. (2022), the computational time for obtaining statistical power using the simulation-based approach for the simplest proposed model (i.e., the longitudinal actor-partner interdependence model with fixed intercepts only) took over three hours when using an Intel Core i7-7820HQ processor. This computational burden poses limitations to the implementation of the simulation-based approach, especially since usually multiple potential sample sizes have to be evaluated. For example, for complicated models, this approach can only realistically be applied via large-scale computers (see e.g., Strubell et al. (2019) for a discussion on resources used by complex computational approaches).

In this article, we provide a way out by returning to the analytic approach to power calculations for multilevel models with autocorrelated errors. Specifically, we focus on deriving analytical formulas for the standard error estimates that can be used for computing the statistical power of Wald-type tests for testing single fixed effects for five types of multilevel models in which repeated measurements (Level 1) are nested within persons (Level 2) where within-person errors follow an AR(1) process. These models allow investigating: (i) the effect of a continuous time-varying Level 1 predictor on the mean level of a time-varying outcome; (ii) differences in the mean level of a time-varying outcome between two groups of persons; (iii) the effect of a Level 1 continuous predictor on a time-varying outcome; (iv) interaction effects between a Level 1 and a Level 2 continuous predictors; and (v) differences between two groups of persons with respect to the effect of a continuous Level 1 predictor on a time-varying outcome. For these models, we show that when the number of persons and the number of repeated measurement occasions per person is sufficiently large, we can obtain a closed-form expression of the standard error of the fixed effect estimates by deriving and approximating the information matrix of the fixed effect estimates of two-level models with autocorrelated errors. Using this closed-form expression, we use the analytic approach to compute statistical power for fixed effects in multilevel models with AR(1) errors, without having to fit the model to large amounts of simulated datasets.

In the remainder of the article, we first recap the analytic and simulation-based approach for conducting power analysis. Next, we analytically derive the precision matrix of five multilevel models that assume within-person errors are autocorrelated, and we validate the analytical approach by comparing its performance with the simulation-based approach. We conclude this paper with a general discussion.
2 Recap of the approaches for the computation of statistical power for multilevel models without AR(1) errors

In this section, we are going to juxtapose two approaches for conducting power analysis via an empirical example. The first approach is the simulation-based approach, which is currently implemented in the shiny app PowerAnalysisIL (Lafit et al., 2021). The second one is the analytical approach which, prior to this paper, has only been developed for multilevel models without AR(1) errors. In this example, it will be shown in detail how to conduct an a priori power analysis for the statistical test of a fixed effect of interest in a simple two-level regression model via the analytical and via the simulation-based approach.

div.head: The data and the simple model
div.p: To demonstrate the two approaches for the computation of statistical power, we are going to use the popularity data set included in Hox et al. (2017). The popularity data set includes data from 2000 pupils in 100 classes. The main variables of interest are pupil popularity (measured on a scale from one to ten) and teacher experience (measured in years) (see Hox et al., 2017). This study showed that between-class differences in pupil popularity are associated with differences in teacher experience, suggesting that more experienced teachers facilitate stronger classroom ties. But are those findings replicable? Researcher Jane wants to conduct a new study to conceptually replicate this finding. To help Jane with her power analysis, we first need to know how she intends to test the substantive hypothesis that teacher experience is associated with pupil popularity once the data have been gathered. Jane models the popularity score y ij of pupil j = (1, . . . , n i ) in class i = (1, . . . , N ) as
div.formula: y ij = β 00 + β 01 w i + ν 0i + ϵ ij (1)

In equation ( 1), β 00 denotes the fixed intercept and represents the average popularity level in a class where the teacher has no experience. The parameter β 01 represents the influence of the class-level predictor, teacher experiencefoot_0 , such that if β 01 is positive, the average popularity is larger in classes with more experienced teachers. Conversely, if β 01 is negative, the average popularity is lower in classes with more experienced teachers. To allow for additional between-class differences in the average level of popularity, we include the random variable ν 0i , which represents the random intercept of class i. If ν 0i is positive (negative), the average popularity in class i is larger (smaller) than the average popularity level in the population. The random intercept is assumed to be normally distributed with mean zero and variance σ 2 ν 0 . The random variable ϵ ji represents the Level 1 or within-class errors of pupil j in class i. To this end, she has to specify how large she expects the true effect β * 01 to be. To select the true effect, Jane considers the findings of previous research. She is not aware of any other data besides the popularity data set and she has no strong prior beliefs about realistic effect sizes. Because of this, she decides to simply use the point estimate from the popularity data, which is displayed in Table 1, to compute statistical powerfoot_2 .

Since the covariance matrix of β is the inverse of the precision matrix of the vector of fixed effects P β, she could use algebra to calculate SE( β01 ) via P β. However, there are two obstacles. Firstly, P β depends on two model parameters: σ 2 ϵ , σ 2 ν 0 (see Appendix A). Secondly, this matrix depends on two statistics namely the sample mean and the sample variance of the Level 2 predictor. So, what is Jane to do?

To tackle the first problem, Jane can do what is typically done when conducting power analysis which is replacing unknown parameters with educated guesses. To tackle the latter, Jane can respectively replace the sample mean with the population mean and the sample variance with the population variance, knowing that the sample moments converge almost surely to population moments. Therefore, Jane needs to provide values for four unknown quantities: σ 2 ϵ , σ 2 ν 0 , µ w , and σ 2 w . Assuming for simplicity that n i = n ∀ i, Jane will arrive at the following matrix (see Snijders and Bosker, 1993, for a proof):
div.formula: P * β := n σ 2 ϵ + σ 2 ν 0 n N N µ w N µ w (N -1)σ 2 w + N µ 2 w .(10)
div.p: By determining the sample sizes of the replication study as N = 150 and n = 20 and by replacing the unknown parameters in (10) with their point estimates from the popularity data set (see Table 1), P * β becomes a known, real-valued (2 × 2) matrix. Jane can then finally compute SE( β01 ) = 0.01 by taking the square root of the second diagonal element of the inverse of P * β. Plugging it into equation ( 9) then yields a statistical power of 1.00 for α = 0.05.

Unsure of whether this power estimate equal to one is plausible, Jane goes on to also compute statistical power using the simulation-based approach. She sets the number of classes to N = 150 and the number of pupils per class to n = 20. Just like in the analytic approach, Jane needs to assume values for the four unknown quantities σ 2 ϵ , σ 2 ν 0 , µ w , and σ 2 w . As mentioned before, she assumes that those values are equal to the point estimates of the popularity data set (see Table 1). Having done so, she generates 1000 random data sets via Monte Carlo simulation. Afterward, model ( 1) is fitted to each generated dataset using REML. The resulting estimate of the fixed effect β01 and its standard error estimate SE( β01 ) are then used to compute the t-ratio and the p-value (under H 0 , the t-ratio follows a t-distribution with N -2 = 148 degrees of freedom). Finally, the number of generated datasets for which the null hypothesis is rejected is divided by 1000 to yield an estimate of the statistical power. The simulation-based approach yields an estimate of statistical power equal to 1.00. The average standard error of β01 across the 1000 Monte Carlo replicates is 0.01. The total computational time in seconds of the simulation-based approach is 28.79foot_4 .

Note that in Jane's example, the simulation and the analytical approach yield the same power estimate (when rounded to the third decimal). However, power estimates will not always be that similar. The analytic approach assumes values for the unknown model parameters and builds on asymptotic assumptions. In contrast, The simulation-based approach also assumes values for the unknown model parameters but instead of relying on asymptotic theory, it estimates power based on the estimated model parameters for the generated data sets whose sampling distributions depend on the sample size. Given that enough data samples are used in the simulation-based approach, it will therefore yield a more accurate power estimate than the analytical approach. Whereas the simulation power estimate is unbiased, the analytical estimate is not. Ceteris paribus, the smaller N or n, the larger the bias of the analytical estimate. Why would Jane ever want to use the analytical approach then? Although the analytical approach is biased, its bias is negligible when N and n are sufficiently large. Up to a certain number of sampled datasets in the simulation-based approach, the analytical estimate is therefore more accurate 7 . As will be shown, the number of simulated datasets required for the simulation estimate to be more accurate than the analytical one can be quite large which is why the computational burden of the simulation-based approach can be non-negligible. In the next section, we investigate the differences between the two approaches for various sample sizes.
3 Precision matrix for two-level models with autocorrelated errors

In the previous section, we showed that the standard error of the fixed effect estimates is a crucial element in the analytical computation of statistical power. We also demonstrated that to compute the standard error estimate of the fixed effect, we first need to estimate the precision matrix. Therefore, in this section, we showed that given certain assumptions, we can derive an analytical expression of the precision matrix for a set of models that are popular in IL designs. For simplicity of description, these algebraic derivations of the precision matrix are included in Appendix A.

Concretely, we focus on five two-level models with autocorrelated errors, which are widely used to study individual differences in IL studies and properly account for the temporal dependency (see e.g., Lafit et al., 2021). The first model includes a Level 2 or timeinvariant continuous predictor that allows investigating changes in the mean level of an outcome due to changes in the person-level predictor. As such, this model only differs from the simple two-level model that Jane used in that the within-persons follow an AR(1) process. The second model includes a Level 2 binary predictor to estimate differences in the mean level of the outcome between two groups of persons. The third model estimates the fixed within-person association between a Level 1 or time-varying predictor and the outcome. The fourth model extends the third model by including a Level 2 continuous predictor to investigate cross-level interaction effects between the time-varying predictor and the time-invariant predictor. The last model extends the third model by including a binary Level 2 predictor to estimate group differences in the within-persons associations between the time-varying predictor and the outcome. A summary of the models is included in Table 2.

To illustrate how we can use the analytical derivations to compute statistical power we use the clinical data set reported on by Heininga et al. (2019). This data set includes 38 individuals diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD) and 40 control subjects. Participants took part in an ESM study of 7 days. div.head: Illustration
div.p: To compare the results of the analytical and simulation-based approaches, we used the data set from the clinical study to obtain plausible values of the parameters of the model in equation ( 11 Next, we compute the power to test the hypothesis that persons who reported higher levels of depression have on average larger mean NA levels (i.e., H 1 : β 01 > 0). To test this hypothesis, we set the value of α to 5%, the number of persons to 20, 30, 60, 80, 100, 200, and, 300, and the number of (equal) measurement occasions per person to 20, 70, and 140. In addition, to investigate how much statistical power varied as a function of the value of the main effect of interest, we conducted a sensitivity analysis varying the value of β * 01 . First, we conducted the analysis using the estimated value from the clinical data set (i.e., β * 01 = 1.5). Since statistical power is positively associated with the value of β * 01 , we investigated the impact of smaller effect sizes by also running the analysis with β * 01 = 0.15 which corresponds to a 90% decrease in effect size. In the simulation-based approach, we follow the approach described in Lafit et al. div.p: where β 00 is the fixed intercept and β 10 is the fixed slope representing the overall (i.e., across all persons) effect of anhedonia on NA. Between-person differences in the relation between Anhedonia and NA are captured by including a random intercept ν 0i and random slope ν 1i . div.head: Discussion
div.p: Properly powered studies mitigate the chances of false negative findings and gross overand underestimation of effect sizes. Therefore, running power analyses when designing a study contributes to the replicability and generalizability of scientific findings (see Ioannidis, 2005;Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017). To aid researchers working with IL designs, we derived closed-form expressions for the precision matrix of the fixed effects of five different multilevel models that handle the serial dependence in the data. Furthermore, we derived asymptotic approximations of those matrices that do not depend on sample statistics under the assumption that the number of measurement occasions is equal across persons. We then demonstrated how these formulas allow researchers to conduct a power analysis for NHST of the fixed effects. To validate this approach to power analysis, we compared it to the simulation-based approach as done in Lafit et al. (2021) using Monte-Carlo simulations. We found no or only minor differences in power estimates showcasing that the analytical formulas provided are useful as they free researchers from the computational burden of the simulation-based approach.

A first direction for future research is related to the assumption that the number of measurement occasions and persons is sufficiently large. As we showed in the illustrations, when the number of persons or the number of repeated measurements are small the differences between the analytic and the simulation-based approach increase. How large the sample size has to be for the differences between the two approaches to be small likely depends on the model under study and the true values of the model parameters, therefore, it is not possible to provide general rules of thumb in this regard.

Secondly, we note that in this paper only focused on five commonly used models in IL research. Although, we did not investigate the potential of the analytical derivations for other types of models, future research could focus on deriving analytical formulas for the precision matrix of more complex models. Note that (27) shows the precision matrix of a model that includes P Level 1 predictors and multiple cross-level interaction effects. This result can be the starting point for the derivation of analytical formulas that can be used to compute statistical power for more complex models.

A third research direction pertains to the impact of having different numbers of measurement occasions across persons and having unequal time intervals between measurements (such as night breaks). Concerning the first issue, future research could investigate under which conditions it is still possible to obtain a closed-form expression of the precision matrix of the fixed effects. For example, if there are subgroups of individuals with the same number of measurement occasions, the precision matrix of the fixed effects can be computed as the average of the precision matrices in each of the subgroups. Concerning the second issue, the multilevel models presented in this paper cannot accommodate unequal time intervals in the data. In the N = 1 case, Adolf et al. (2021) derived analytical expressions for the covariance matrix for the continuous-time autoregressive model estimators to obtain the optimal sampling rate. This framework could be extended to the multilevel case to accommodate unequal time intervals.

A fourth research direction concerns which null hypothesis is tested. In this paper, we only focused on null hypothesis tests of fixed effects of interest. Future research could use the analytical approximations of the precision matrix derived in this paper to obtain statistical power for variance component testing (see e.g., Berkhof and Snijders, 2001).

A final direction for future research concerns the uncertainty in the parameter estimates used for conducting power analysis. For multilevel models, power analysis is often conducted using pilot data or data from previous studies to obtain the values of the model parameters (Lane and Hennes, 2018). This can result in uncertainty about sample size recommendations in case of large uncertainty in the parameter estimates based on these data (e.g., when using data from a small pilot study). Future research could investigate the impact of uncertainty about the true values of the model parameters by conducting sensitivity analyses (see e.g., Lafit et al., 2022;Lane andHennes, 2018, 2019). Given the low computational burden of the analytic approach, such sensitivity analyses can be easily implemented. We also note that assumptions about the distribution of the Level 1 and Level 2 predictors are needed to compute statistical power with the simulation-based or the analytic approach. Violations of these assumptions can severely impact sample size recommendations. Thus, sensitivity analyses can also be performed to investigate the impact of violations of the distributional assumptions about the model's predictors on statistical power.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The current study introduced asymptotic approximations of the precision matrix for multilevel models with autocorrelated errors. These approximations can be used to conduct statistical power analyses without any computational burden.
